newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S. Korean refinery costs up on new pollution laws.
newsitem.headline: S. Korean refinery costs up on new pollution laws.

text.p: Tougher pollution laws that came into effect in South Korea on Tuesday could add millions of dollars in costs to refineries, analysts said.

New government laws on sulphur in oil products means that the South Korean refining sector -- the third biggest in Asia after Japan and China -- has to choose between buying more expensive low-sulphur crude oil or investing in units that filter the sulphur out.
And the refiners appear to be choosing for now buying low sulphur crude rather than further expansion.
But both options would be costly, they said.

As of July 1, sulphur in fuel oil has been cut to 0.5 percent from 1.0 percent in urban areas, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said. The reduction will spread to most cities and counties from July 1, 1999.
Diesel for industrial and home use nationwide must have a sulphur content of just 0.1 percent. The level is currently enforced only in urban areas.
In April 1998, the sulphur content in diesel for cars will be cut to 0.05 percent from 0.1 percent.

Low sulphur crude is more expensive to buy than higher sulphur crude because supplies are more limited. An average tanker of 900,000 barrels of low sulphur crude could costs $2/$3 more per barrel that high sulphur crude, adding $1.8-$2.7 million per tanker.

Increasingly Asia is looking to West Africa to meet its demand, because Asian supplies are so tight. South Korea is Asia's biggest buyer of West African crude, taking more than one quarter of West African imports.
Building desulphurising units would be a better solution for the long term but refiners are hesitant to pay for such costly projects.
"Refiners are not thrilled about building new desulphurising facilities because the cost is really high," a ministry official said.
The new units would cost each refiner in the range of $70-$140 million, industry sources said.

"No new plans for desulphurisers have been introduced despite toughening regulations," the official said. "Refiners don't think it's economical to set up new desulphurisers. They'd prefer to buy more low-sulphur crude."
The rapid growth of South Korea's refining sector has not included much desulphurisation capacity.
South Korea has fuel oil desulphurisation capacity of 65,000 bpd, the ministry said. The sector has plans to raise the fuel oil desulphurisation capacity to 155,000 bpd by early 2000.
Middle distillate desulphurisation capacity, including diesel, is 549,000 bpd and will be raised to 659,000 bpd by 1998.
But domestic demand is already outstripping that level.
Government data showed expected demand for fuel oil at 442,000 bpd middle distillates at 719,500 bpd in 1997.
Traders said South Korea could start importing fuel oil with 0.5-percent sulphur, but the amount was likely to be limited.
"Our basic policy is to rely on low sulphur crude rather than the product," said a trader at Hyundai Oil Refinery Co.
A trader at Yukong Ltd said: "South Korea's dependence on West African crude is expected to grow sharply in line with the new law."
Moreover, industry officials and refiners saw a rise in exports of higher sulphur fuel oil, which would be targetted mostly for China and southeast Asia.
--Seoul Newsroom (+822 727 5643)
